titulo: Module 10 — Quiz: context management and prompt caching

questoes.pergunta: Why does a long conversation get more expensive with each turn on the Messages API?
opcoes: Because the model charges a fixed per-turn fee that grows with the number of turns
Because the API is stateless: the entire history is resent and billed on every request
Because the model generates longer responses as the history grows
Because the prompt cache expires at the end of each turn and the entire prefix has to be written again, at the write premium
questoes.explicacao: The Messages API keeps no state: each request carries the full history, and all those input tokens are billed again (except whatever comes from the cache).
feedbacks: There's no per-turn fee; billing is per token.
Correct. Stateless = resending and paying for the history on every turn.
Response length doesn't grow because of the history; the cost comes from the resent input.
The cache doesn't expire every turn (TTL of minutes, refreshed on read); and caching makes things cheaper, not more expensive.

questoes.pergunta: A critical rule ('never refund above 500 without approval') sits in the middle of a 30,000-token system prompt and is sometimes ignored. What is the most direct context fix?
opcoes: Switch to a model with a larger window, so the 30,000-token prompt takes up a smaller fraction of the context
Repeat the rule at several points in the middle of the prompt
Increase max_tokens so the model has room to reason
Move the rule to the beginning, under a clear heading (and enforce it in code)
questoes.explicacao: Lost in the middle: information in the middle of long contexts receives less attention. Place what's critical at the beginning, under a heading. And a critical financial rule should be enforced in code (a hook), not just in the prompt.
feedbacks: A larger window doesn't improve attention to the middle; it tends to make it worse, and it costs more.
Repeating it in the middle still leaves it in the middle; and it adds noise.
max_tokens limits the output; it doesn't change attention to the input.
Correct. Position and structure attack lost in the middle; code guarantees the rule.

questoes.pergunta: After an automatic summary, the support agent started calling process_refund with the wrong order_id. What is the recommended fix?
opcoes: Keep a CASE FACTS block (IDs, amounts, dates) outside the summary and reinject it on every turn
Instruct the summarizer to 'preserve all important details, especially IDs and amounts', and review the summary prompt
Disable summarization and let the conversation grow indefinitely
Ask the customer for the order_id again on every tool call
questoes.explicacao: Summaries lose exact values and IDs. Transactional facts go in a persistent case facts block that is never summarized.
feedbacks: Correct. Case facts take the exact data out of the summary's reach.
Summarization is still probabilistic; this is the anti-pattern of trusting the summary.
The conversation will overflow the window and degrade; it doesn't solve anything.
A terrible experience, and it doesn't attack the cause (loss in the summary).

questoes.pergunta: In Claude Code, which of these is MOST likely to be lost after a /compact?
opcoes: The contents of the project's CLAUDE.md
The most recent messages in the conversation, which are the first to be summarized by /compact
The literal error message from a stack trace read at the start of the session
What was written to the memory file
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.md, the system prompt, recent messages, and memory survive. Old details, early tool results, and exact text (such as error messages) can be lost.
feedbacks: CLAUDE.md is reloaded; it survives.
Recent messages are preserved.
Correct. Exact text from the start of the session is the kind of detail a summary loses.
Memory lives on disk; it survives.

questoes.pergunta: What is a typical sign of context degradation in a long codebase-exploration session?
opcoes: The agent starts using Grep instead of Read
The agent asks for permission to edit files
The agent starts creating subagents for parallel tasks instead of doing the exploration directly in the main session
Vague answers like 'follows the typical patterns' instead of citing the specific class already read
questoes.explicacao: Signs of degradation: generic answers instead of specific code, inconsistency, and forgetting earlier findings.
feedbacks: Using Grep is healthy exploration, not degradation.
Asking for permission is permission-mode behavior, not a context signal.
Delegating to subagents is a mitigation, not a symptom.
Correct. Generic where it should be specific is the classic symptom.

questoes.pergunta: A long-running coordinator needs to be able to resume work if the process crashes midway. What should you implement?
opcoes: A manifest in a known location with tasks, status, and paths to partial results
A lower iteration limit
A 1-hour cache TTL
A system prompt asking the model to 'remember where it left off' and resume from the last completed task
questoes.explicacao: State saved in a known location + the coordinator's manifest let a new session read it and resume after a crash.
feedbacks: Correct. The state needs to live outside the conversation.
An iteration limit doesn't save state.
Caching isn't persistence of work state.
The model has no memory across processes; a prompt doesn't save state.

questoes.pergunta: An agent makes hundreds of search calls; the old results have already been synthesized and just take up space. Which mechanism is the most appropriate?
opcoes: Memory tool, moving the old results into files outside the conversation
Compaction
Case facts block
Context editing (clearing old tool results)
questoes.explicacao: Context editing clears old tool results (and/or thinking). Ideal for verbose agentic loops whose results have already been consumed.
feedbacks: The memory tool persists across sessions; it doesn't reduce the current context.
Compaction summarizes the narrative; here it's enough to discard results already used.
Case facts store exact values; they don't free up space.
Correct. Clearing stale tool results is exactly the use case.

questoes.pergunta: The team enabled server-side compaction, but the history keeps growing until it overflows. The code does messages.Add(response.Content[0].Text). What is the cause?
opcoes: The compaction threshold is too high; it needs to be lowered so it fires before the history grows
It appends only the text and discards the compaction block; you need to append the entire response.content
Compaction doesn't work with tools
A cache breakpoint is missing on the last block
questoes.explicacao: With compaction, the response carries a compaction block. Extracting only the text silently loses that state.
feedbacks: Even with an appropriate threshold, the discarded block keeps compaction from taking effect.
Correct. Append the entire response.content.
Compaction works in loops with tools.
Caching has nothing to do with the history's growth.

questoes.pergunta: Which mechanism makes preferences discovered about a customer available at the NEXT support interaction, days later?
opcoes: Memory tool (persistent files outside the conversation)
Context editing
Compaction, which summarizes the previous interaction into a reusable block
Prompt caching with a 1-hour TTL
questoes.explicacao: The memory tool stores findings in files that persist across sessions; you implement the storage.
feedbacks: Correct. Persistence across sessions.
Context editing deletes; it doesn't persist anything.
Compaction lives inside a single conversation.
Caching isn't business memory, and it expires in minutes/1 hour.

questoes.pergunta: What is the essential difference between task budget and max_tokens?
opcoes: Task budget is billed in dollars; max_tokens in tokens
Task budget is visible to the model, which organizes itself to fit; max_tokens is invisible and cuts off midway
Task budget applies only to the Batch API
max_tokens limits the entire agentic task; task budget limits each individual response and cuts off when it hits the ceiling
questoes.explicacao: Visible ceiling → the model plans and finishes in an orderly way. Invisible ceiling → truncation with stop_reason max_tokens.
feedbacks: Both are measured in tokens.
Correct.
It has nothing to do with the Batch API.
Reversed: max_tokens is per response; task budget is for the agentic task.

questoes.pergunta: How does a safety refusal reach your code on the Messages API?
opcoes: As HTTP 400 with type invalid_request_error
As HTTP 403
As HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal'
As a timeout exception in the SDK
questoes.explicacao: The refusal arrives with HTTP 200 and stop_reason refusal. That's why you need to check stop_reason before reading content.
feedbacks: 400 is for a malformed request, not a refusal.
403 is permissions/authentication.
Correct. Success status, refusal content.
A refusal isn't a timeout.

questoes.pergunta: In what order is the prompt caching prefix rendered?
opcoes: system → tools → messages
messages → system → tools
tools → system → messages
Order doesn't matter; the cache works per independent block
questoes.explicacao: tools → system → messages. A change to the tools invalidates the cached system and messages.
feedbacks: Tools come before system.
Messages are the final part of the prefix.
Correct.
The cache matches the exact prefix; order is everything.

questoes.pergunta: The system prompt starts with 'Now: 2026-10-11T14:02:37Z' and has cache_control at the end. What happens?
opcoes: The cache works normally, because the timestamp is short
The cache automatically ignores dates in the prefix
The API returns a 400, because variable content isn't allowed inside a block marked with cache_control
Every request pays for a cache write and there's never a read, because the prefix always changes
questoes.explicacao: Any differing byte in the prefix invalidates the cache. With a timestamp in the system prompt, every request writes and none reads: it ends up more expensive than not caching at all.
feedbacks: Size doesn't matter; a single differing byte is enough.
There's no date normalization; matching is exact.
There's no error: the invalidation is silent.
Correct. A classic silent invalidator.

questoes.pergunta: Repeated requests show cache_read_input_tokens = 0 and cache_creation_input_tokens = 0, with cache_control on a ~300-token system prompt. What is the most likely cause?
opcoes: A prefix below the model's minimum cacheable length: it silently doesn't cache
A timestamp in the system prompt
The 5-minute TTL expired between requests and the cache was discarded before being read
Too many breakpoints
questoes.explicacao: If not even the write happens, the prefix didn't reach the minimum cacheable length. Below the minimum there's no error, just zero.
feedbacks: Correct. Zero writes point to a prefix that's too small.
A timestamp would cause a write on every request (creation > 0), not zero.
An expired TTL would cause a new write, not zero.
More than 4 breakpoints would produce an error, not silence.

questoes.pergunta: Which of these does NOT invalidate prompt caching?
opcoes: Building the tools list dynamically per request
Serializing the system prompt from a dictionary with nondeterministic key order
Placing the user's question after the last breakpoint
Including the session ID at the beginning of the system prompt
questoes.explicacao: Putting the volatile part after the last breakpoint is exactly the correct design. The other three are silent invalidators.
feedbacks: Varying tools change the start of the prefix: it invalidates everything.
Unstable key order changes the prefix's bytes.
Correct. Stable first, volatile after.
A session ID in the prefix makes each session a different prefix.
